events.description: Emergency department presentation with history, vitals and abdominal examination; concern for strangulation/peritonitis

evidence.quote: A 44-year-old African American woman presented to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of progressively worsening abdominal pain, persistent nausea, multiple episodes of bilious emesis, and complete absence of flatus or bowel movements. She described the pain as diffuse, crampy, and increasingly severe since onset. Her past medical and surgical histories were unremarkable, and she reported no chronic illnesses or prior abdominal operations. The only noted allergy was to ACE inhibitors, which previously caused angioedema. She denied chest pain, dyspnea, hematochezia, or urinary symptoms.

events.description: Admission laboratory/urine/pregnancy results, including conflicting electrolyte/BUN interpretation

evidence.quote: Laboratory evaluation on admission (Table 1) revealed a leukocytosis of 14,900/µL with marked neutrophil predominance (82%), consistent with an acute inflammatory or infectious process. Hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelet counts were within normal limits. Serum electrolytes were unremarkable, and both blood urea nitrogen and creatinine levels were within normal ranges, indicating preserved renal function despite ongoing vomiting. Liver enzymes and bilirubin were also normal. A mildly elevated serum lactate of 2.4 mmol/L raised concern for early tissue hypoperfusion or evolving bowel compromise in the setting of suspected obstruction. A urine pregnancy test was negative, and urinalysis was largely unremarkable aside from trace ketones, likely reflecting reduced oral intake.

events.description: Acute surgical abdomen prompted emergency operating-room exploration with imaging deferred

evidence.quote: Given the evolving peritonitic manifestations, leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance, and rising concern for bowel compromise, the clinical picture was consistent with an acute surgical abdomen. To avoid delaying definitive intervention, additional imaging was deferred, and the patient was taken emergently to the operating room for exploratory surgery and definitive management.

events.description: Emergency open repair:4cm defect/ischemic omentum, viable bowel, partial omentectomy and primary closure without mesh

evidence.quote: Upon entering the abdominal cavity, a 4-cm ventral fascial defect was recognized, incorporating a tightly incarcerated omentum with evidence of venous congestion and early ischemic changes. The involved omental segment was firmly adherent within the hernia sac, preventing reduction of the hernia. Careful dissection was accomplished to free the ensnared tissue, followed by reduction of the hernia contents (Figure 1). The nonviable portion of the omentum was resected (Figure 2), and the specimen was sent for pathologic evaluation. Given the emergent setting, the presence of ischemic and necrotic omental tissue, and the increased risk of mesh infection in a potentially contaminated field, the decision was made to perform primary fascial closure using non-absorbable sutures. Although mesh reinforcement is generally recommended for ventral hernia defects larger than 2 cm to reduce recurrence risk, this approach was deferred in favor of damage-control repair, with consideration for elective definitive reconstruction if clinically indicated. The patient tolerated the procedure without complications.

Upon entering the abdominal cavity, a 4-cm ventral fascial defect was recognized, incorporating a tightly incarcerated omentum with evidence of venous congestion and early ischemic changes.

Pathologic examination of the resected omental specimen demonstrated benign fibroadipose tissue with focal areas of congestion and hemorrhage, consistent with ischemic changes secondary to incarceration (Figure 3).

summary.text: A 44-year-old African American woman with no reported chronic illnesses, prior abdominal operations, known hernia or obesity presented with 24 hours of worsening diffuse crampy abdominal pain, persistent nausea, bilious vomiting and obstipation. ACE inhibitors had caused angioedema. She denied chest pain, dyspnea, hematochezia and urinary symptoms. Arrival temperature was 38.3 °C, pulse 112/min and saturation 98% on room air; a distended tender abdomen with guarding/rebound and a firm nonreducible right-lower abdominal-wall mass raised concern for peritonitis/strangulation. WBC was 14,900/µL with 82% neutrophils, lactate 2.4 mmol/L and trace urinary ketones; pregnancy/other urine screens were negative. Hemoglobin, hematocrit, platelets and liver tests were explicitly reported normal; the differential includes other numeric values without source-stated normality flags. Numeric electrolyte/renal values were preserved, while normal versus abnormal interpretations conflict between narrative/table caption. Imaging was deferred for emergent open exploration. A 4 cm fascial defect trapped adherent congested/ischemic omentum; bowel was viable. The hernia contents were released/reduced, nonviable omentum and hernia sac excised, and fascia closed with nonabsorbable sutures. Mesh was deferred for potential contamination/infection risk; elective reconstruction was only conditionally considered. Histology showed benign fibroadipose/fibrocollagenous tissue with congestion, hemorrhage and dilated vessels, without malignancy or necrotizing infection. The course was uncomplicated, with postoperative day 3 discharge after oral tolerance, pain control and return of bowel function. At two weeks the incision healed appropriately and normal activities resumed without new concerns or recurrent symptoms. Adhesive obstruction, internal hernia, malignancy and volvulus were lower-likelihood author-discussed differentials, not confirmed conditions.
